{
  "research_question": "Do mouse navigation performance metrics (Time-to-Target, Success, Path Efficiency, Average Speed, and Angular Dispersion) differ significantly across five stimulation paradigms: Combined, ICMS Only, Dim Visual Only, Bright Visual Only, and Sham?",
  "stim_paradigms_compared": [
    "Combined",
    "ICMS Only",
    "Dim Visual Only",
    "Bright Visual Only",
    "Sham"
  ],
  "response_variables": [
    "Time-to-Target",
    "Success",
    "Path Efficiency",
    "Average Speed",
    "AD"
  ],
  "anova_plan": [
    "Perform a one-way Analysis of Variance (ANOVA) for each of the five response variables to test the null hypothesis that the mean performance metric is equal across the five stimulation paradigms.",
    "Prior to ANOVA, verify normality of residuals per group and homogeneity of variances (homoscedasticity). If variances are unequal, apply Welch's ANOVA.",
    "For 'Success', convert to binary (0 or 1) and perform a One-Way Chi-Square Test for Independence (or Cochran-Mantel-Haenszel if stratification by Mouse ID is required due to pseudoreplication) instead of ANOVA.",
    "If data exhibits significant outliers or non-normal distributions despite transformations, use Kruskal-Wallis H tests as the non-parametric alternative for all continuous variables.",
    "Model the data accounting for the nested structure where multiple trials occur per Mouse, likely requiring a Mixed-Effects Linear Model (MMANOVA/MLM) with 'Mouse' as a random intercept to avoid pseudoreplication, treating 'Stim Paradigm' as a fixed effect."
  ],
  "assumptions_and_diagnostics": [
    "Normality: Assess via visual inspection of Q-Q plots of residuals and Shapiro-Wilk tests for each stimulation group.",
    "Homogeneity of Variances: Assess via Levene's Test or Bartlett's Test.",
    "Independence: Verify that trials within a Mouse are correctly accounted for (nested design) rather than treated as independent observations; if treating trials as independent, the validity is suspect due to potential within-subject correlation.",
    "No Extreme Outliers: Check boxplots for extreme values, particularly in 'Time-to-Target' and 'Path Efficiency' which have high ranges (min/max ratios >100)."
  ],
  "posthoc_plan": [
    "If the omnibus ANOVA (or WWelch/Kruskal-Wallis) yields a p-value < 0.05, proceed to pairwise comparisons.",
    "Use Tukey's HSD (Honestly Significant Difference) test for pairwise mean differences to control the family-wise error rate.",
    "If using Welch's ANOVA due to heteroscedasticity, use Games-Howell post-hoc tests.",
    "If using Kruskal-Wallis, perform Dunn's test with Bonferroni correction for pairwise rank comparisons.",
    "Report effect sizes (Cohen's f for ANOVA, Cliff's delta for non-parametric) alongside p-values."
  ],
  "expected_findings": [
    "Significant differences are expected in 'Time-to-Target' and 'Success' between 'Combined' vs. 'Sham' and potentially between visual-only paradigms depending on navigating conditions.",
    " 'ICMS Only' may show intermediate or superior performance compared to visual-only conditions if stimulation aids sensory integration.",
    " 'Path Efficiency' and 'Average Speed' may vary significantly, with 'Combined' potentially showing lower efficiency (more exploratory) but higher success rates.",
    "'AD' (Angular Dispersion) is expected to differ if stimulation stabilizes navigation paths, showing potentially lower dispersion in enhanced paradigms."
  ],
  "limitations": [
    "The dataset contains 76,655 rows, likely representing multiple trials per Mouse (n=8 levels). Standard ANOVA assumes independence, which is violated if trials are nested within Mice, necessitating mixed models rather than simple ANOVA to avoid inflated Type I error rates.",
    " 'Success' is binary; applying ANOVA to binary outcomes is statistically inappropriate (violates normality and homoscedasticity assumptions); a logistic regression or Chi-square test is required.",
    "'Path Efficiency' has a very wide range (0.0009 to 29.8), suggesting a highly skewed distribution that likely violates normality assumptions without transformation.",
    "The 'Combined' condition has a vastly larger sample size (48,846) compared to others (min 3,323), which can artificially reduce standard errors and bias variance estimates if not modeled correctly."
  ],
  "recommended_next_analysis": "Fit a Linear Mixed-Effects Model (LMM) for each response variable (except Success, which requires GLMM) with 'Stim Paradigm' as a fixed effect and 'Mouse' as a random intercept to account for the nested trial structure. For 'Success', use a Binomial GLMM. This approach provides more accurate inference regarding the effect of stimulation paradigms while correcting for pseudoreplication."
}
